description: The Public Service Commission of the District of Columbia, in Consumer Complaint No. 2025-9075277, by Order No. 22889, dated June 30, 2026, affirmed the Dismissal Order of the Hearing Officer and denied the Complainant’s Objection, Exceptions, and Petition for Review of Order Dismissing Formal Hearing Complaint.
text:
PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION OF THE DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA 
1325 G STREET N.W., SUITE 800 
WASHINGTON, D.C. 20005 
ORDER ON APPEAL 
June 30, 2026 
CONSUMER COMPLAINT NO. CC 2025-9075277 – LEVINSON V. POTOMAC 
ELECTRIC POWER COMPANY, Order No. 22889 
I.
INTRODUCTION
1.
This matter is an appeal from a Hearing Officer decision dismissing a
consumer complaint filed by Rebecca Levinson (“Complainant” or “Ms. Levinson”) 
against the Potomac Electric Power Company (“Pepco” or “Company”).1 By this Order, 
the Public Service Commission of the District of Columbia (“Commission”) affirms the 
Dismissal Order of the Hearing Officer and denies the Appeal. 
II.
BACKGROUND
2.
The following facts are undisputed. Complainant installed a photovoltaic
system on her home and uses a solar energy generation app to monitor and manage what 
her system is doing. In July 2024, Pepco granted Complainant authorization to connect 
her system to the energy grid, which allows her to participate in net metering and receive 
a credit for the solar generated energy she produces in excess of the grid energy that she 
consumes. That same month, Complainant advised Pepco that she didn’t think Pepco’s 
system was properly crediting her for generation. Pepco investigated the matter and 
discovered a system communication error, which Pepco corrected in August 2024. 
3.
In October 2024, Pepco discovered another system error that resulted in
Complainant being underbilled for consumption and revised her bills. The revised billing 
included a calculation that Complainant’s excess kWh generation balance through 
October 23, 2024, to be 145 kWh. However, upon further investigation, Pepco 
discovered yet another error, this one caused the daily register readings for her generation 
to be undercounted by a factor of ten. Therefore, in December 2024, Pepco revised 
Complainant’s billing to reflect an upward adjustment of generation from 145 kWh to 
1,449 kWh. 
4.
Complainant wasn’t convinced that Pepco had properly credited her

generation so, in February 2025, she filed a complaint with the Commission demanding 
that Pepco provide her with a detailed accounting of her bills. In response, Pepco 
acknowledged its mistakes and explained that part of the confusion is that Complainant is 
trying to be credited for energy that she generated before being authorized to connect to 
the grid. Although Pepco says that energy generated before approval to connect to the 
grid is not subject to credit under its NEM tariff, as a gesture of goodwill, Pepco said that 
it would credit her for an additional 19 kWh. Unfortunately, a ‘scrivener’s error’ recorded 
the credit as 19,000 kWh, creating another mistake that Pepco had to correct. Even so, 
Pepco said that it had corrected all its mistakes and adjusted the billing accordingly so 
there’s no relief left for the Commission’s Hearing Officer to give. 

5. 
Complainant continued to believe that she was not properly billed. As the 
matter was still before the Hearing Officer for the 2025 summer billing cycle, 
Complainant suggested using the 2025 billing data in place of data for 2024 on the theory 
that the same calendar months one year apart represent comparable usage. The Hearing 
Officer found no legal basis for this proposal, especially since Pepco had provided him 
with actual data for the period at issue. Having reviewed all of Complainant’s arguments, 
the Hearing Officer found that she had not met her burden of proving that she was 
entitled to more than Pepco had given her and dismissed the case. This appeal followed.2 

III. 
DISCUSSION 

6. 
Complainant is understandably dissatisfied with a billing process riddled 
with errors. However, we agree with the Hearing Officer that Complainant has not 
proved entitlement to more relief than Pepco has already given her. We, therefore, affirm 
the Hearing Officer’s Order and deny the Complainant’s Appeal. 

THEREFORE, IT IS ORDERED THAT: 

7. 
Based on the foregoing, the Dismissal Order of the Hearing Officer is 
AFFIRMED; and 

8. 
The Complainant’s Objection, Exceptions, and Petition for Review of 
Order Dismissing Formal Hearing Complaint is DENIED.
